query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In a single‐phase high-entropy alloy that initially exhibits homogeneous grain and boundary chemistry, service-like thermal and mechanical loading induces a slow, localized decomposition that leads to nanoscale segregation and formation of brittle precipitates at the grain boundaries. This emergent behavior—different from the immediate impurity-driven grain-boundary failure in conventional alloys—degrades toughness over time.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous, single-phase, compositionally complex high-entropy alloy with uniformly distributed elements and no detectable grain-boundary segregation or secondary phases.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to controlled thermal cycling and mechanical fatigue (representative of relevant service conditions) while keeping other environmental variables constant.
generation.conditions: The experiment compares samples under extended thermal cycling and cyclic loading vs. samples maintained in the as-cast state. Measurements are taken at room temperature and at service-relevant elevated temperatures to capture potential low-temperature embrittlement and high-temperature softening transitions.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale precipitate formation or clustering of specific alloying elements localized at or near the grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Under cyclic thermal-mechanical loading, the sluggish diffusion inherent to high-entropy alloys eventually permits local chemical inhomogeneities to develop. These inhomogeneities nucleate nanoprecipitates or clusters at the grain boundaries, acting as stress concentrators and initiating brittle fracture, rather than the rapid segregation seen in conventional alloys.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with the baseline homogeneous state, thermally and mechanically cycled samples will exhibit reduced toughness, evidenced by lower fracture toughness values and the appearance of intergranular fracture features along with detectable nanoscale precipitates at grain boundaries in microstructural analyses.
generation.baseline: The as-cast single-phase high-entropy alloy that exhibits high toughness and homogeneity in grain-boundary chemistry.
generation.boundary: Service conditions involving prolonged thermal cycling and cyclic mechanical loading. The effect is expected to be significant only after a threshold exposure time/number of cycles, beyond which nanoscale chemical segregation becomes appreciable.
generation.uncertainty: The exact kinetics of precipitate nucleation, the critical conditions (temperature, cycle frequency, and amplitude) for onset of brittle behavior, and the specific nature of the nanoscale phases could vary with composition and processing history, which introduces measurement and interpretation uncertainties.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy samples from the same as-cast batch. Subject one set to prolonged thermal cycling combined with cyclic mechanical fatigue (mimicking service conditions) while retaining the second set as a control. After the testing period, analyze both sets using high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) and atom probe tomography (APT) to assess any nanoscale chemical segregations or precipitate formation at grain boundaries, and perform standardized fracture toughness tests.
measurements: Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) for macroscopic fracture features
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and atom probe tomography (APT) for detecting grain-boundary precipitates
Microhardness testing across grains and boundaries
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the exhausted samples under thermal and mechanical loading do not show any statistically significant reduction in fracture toughness compared to the uncycled control and no nanoscale precipitates or clustering are detected at the grain boundaries, the hypothesis that service-induced nanoscale segregation causes brittle behavior in the high-entropy alloy is falsified.
